newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Stricken Mir crew face grim wait for repair.
newsitem.headline: Stricken Mir crew face grim wait for repair.

text.p: The three men aboard Russia's stricken Mir space station prepared on Thursday for a bleak couple of weeks awaiting a relief ship to bring vital supplies needed for the repair of their damaged craft.

Forced to halt experiments and physical exercise after an accident on Wednesday left them badly short of power, American Michael Foale and two Russian colleagues face one of the most difficult crises in space since Apollo 13 came close to disaster in 1970.
Russian Space Agency chief Yuri Koptev said the cosmonauts were in no immediate danger and there were no plans to evacuate them after the worst accident in Mir's 11-year history.

"They feel fine, although they went through a bit of stress yesterday," he told reporters at the Korolyov Mission Control Centre outside Moscow. A Progress cargo craft will be launched in 11 days, carrying supplies to repair the damage, he said.
But the crew will take to their Soyuz escape craft and return to Earth if the air pressure in their main accommodation falls below about three quarters of the current norm, he said.
A docking probe on another Progress freighter pierced a hole in one of Mir's scientific modules, the Spektr, and smashed one of four solar panels, cutting electricity by 25 to 30 percent.
Mission Control said British-born Foale, mission commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin faced a "five-point emergency". A "seven" means abandon ship.

"It will be a darkened ship," said Jerry Linenger, a NASA astronaut. He survived a serious fire on Mir in February which, with the latest incident and other mishaps, have dented confidence in Russia's financially troubled space programme.

Mission Control spokesman Valery Latyshev said all the experiments the crew had planned were cancelled to save power and they would no longer take the oxygen-burning exercise they normally have to do to combat the effects of weightlessness on the body.

Cramped conditions on Mir are far from ideal at the best of times. Foale has described it as "a very dirty and grimy camping trip in an old car". Tension and inactivity will put a premium on good relations among the men. But since the end of the Cold War space race Americans and Russians are no strangers in orbit.

The Soviet-built Mir, which means both "Peace" and "World" in Russian, was caught in a vicious circle. The collision knocked its solar panels out of line with the Sun, reducing its power. And with low power the crew were finding it hard to realign the ungainly 140-tonne complex of interconnecting modules.
The cosmonauts may make a space walk while waiting for the Progress. It was due to start a routine trip on Friday but will now wait 10 more days for supplies at the Baikonur launch pad.
The crew seemed in good spirits from what little of their conversation was audible to reporters at Mission Control. They could be heard laughing during discussions with the experts.
To conserve power, they did not broadcast television pictures. Foale, a 40-year-old physicist on the station since May, said his computer equipment was stuck in the holed Spektr module.

A committee including NASA officials and Mir's designer met for three hours to fix details of the repair mission. Deputy mission chief Sergei Krikalyov told Reuters only Russian supplies, including specialised electric cables, were needed.

Even when the Progress arrives after a two-day journey the crew's problems may not be over. A spokesman for Russia's Military Space Forces, which will launch the Progress, said Mir's low power would make the docking "very difficult".

If the crew were forced to evacuate it would recall memories of the 1970 Apollo 13 mission, when three U.S. astronauts abandoned ship after an explosion. As the world held its breath, they defied lengthy odds and made it home in a tiny lunar landing craft that was short on air, power and heating.
In Mir's case, however, the lifeboat is a state-of-the-art Soyuz TM-25, specifically designed for the return journey.
More of a headache back on Earth would be the fate of the massive Mir complex if it were abandoned. It is too big to burn up in the atmosphere and could fall on a built-up area.

The Russian space programme has come under fire from U.S. politicians concerned for the safety of NASA astronauts and about taxpayers' dollars pumped into the Mir programme as a test-bed for the planned international space station, Alpha.
Moscow and Washington have exchanged harsh words over delays in Russia's part of the project, due to be launched next year.
This is an anxious time for the crews' families. Linenger said recently that after February's fire problems snowballed: "It seemed like every day something else was going wrong."
Foale's father praised the Mir on Thursday and said his son, who is married with two children, should complete his mission.
Russian space officials, following standard practice, would give no family details on Tsibliyev, 43, and Lazutkin, 39.
